caption:
Who actually found the Dead Sea Scrolls?

Between November 1946 and February 1947, three Bedouin — Muhammed edh-Dhib, his cousin Jum'a Muhammed and Khalil Musa — were at the cliffs near Qumran. Jum'a noticed the caves. Edh-Dhib was the first to actually fall into the one now called Cave 1. He came back to camp with a handful of scrolls: Isaiah, the Habakkuk commentary, the Community Rule. None were destroyed.

The scrolls hung on a tent pole while the family decided what to do with them. At some point the Community Rule was split in two. A dealer in Bethlehem handed them back, saying they were worthless. Three were then sold for seven Jordanian pounds, roughly $28.

In 1954 four scrolls were advertised in The Wall Street Journal and sold at the Waldorf-Astoria in New York for $250,000.

Cave 1 itself was then lost for nearly two years, and was only rediscovered on 28 January 1949. Digging went on until 1956: eleven caves, 981 manuscripts. Cave 4 alone produced 90% of everything, torn into about 15,000 pieces. The Book of Esther has never turned up.

Still open: who wrote them. The long-standing answer is the Essenes; other scholars argue for priests in Jerusalem or unknown Jewish groups. Israel's custody of the collection is disputed by Jordan and the Palestinian Authority.

Images: the Qumran cave photographed by Effi Schweizer, 2007; the cave entrance and the pottery jars by Willem van de Poll (Nationaal Archief); the Great Isaiah Scroll photographed by Ardon Bar Hama; Genesis fragment 4Q7; the Temple Scroll, Israel Museum.

cards.headline: This pushed the Hebrew Bible back <y>a thousand years</y>.
cards.note: Before Qumran the oldest Hebrew scriptures were 10th-century Masoretic texts. This scroll is 2nd century BCE.
cards.source: Great Isaiah Scroll, photo Ardon Bar Hama
cards.alt: Three long horizontal strips of an ancient parchment scroll covered in Hebrew columns.

cards.headline: Cave 4 gave up <y>15,000 pieces</y> of 500 texts.
cards.note: That single cave produced 90% of all the scrolls found. This scrap is 4Q7, the start of Genesis.
cards.alt: Torn brown leather scroll fragment with several lines of black Hebrew script.

cards.headline: <y>The scrolls are genuine</y>. The authors are not known.
cards.note: All 16 fragments the Museum of the Bible bought were modern fakes. Who wrote the real ones is still argued.
cards.source: Temple Scroll 11Q19, Israel Museum · public domain
cards.alt: Ragged upper edge of a pale parchment scroll with dense lines of Hebrew writing.
